passage.title: Embers in the Glass House
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Sleet rattled against the sloped glass panes of the school greenhouse while Leo held a fine camel-hair brush between his fingers. For four months, he had tended twelve pots of Cherokee Purple and Brandywine heirloom tomatoes for the county plant show. With brass tweezers, he gently lifted pale pollen from one blossom and dabbed it onto the stigma of the next flower. He tied a tiny white yarn tag around the stem to mark the cross. Outside, the cold January wind howled across the frozen yard, yet the humid air inside smelled of damp soil and green leaves.

Just as Leo closed his notes, the steady hum of the corner fan sputtered and died. Halfway through the midnight storm, the main gas valve feeding the overhead furnace was abruptly snapped shut by a sheet of falling roof ice. Within ten minutes, frost began creeping like white lace across the lower glass panels. Leo checked the wall thermometer and felt his stomach drop as the red line plummeted toward thirty-five degrees. One hard freeze would burst the watery cells in the stems and ruin his delicate blossoms before dawn.

Help would take at least an hour on the slick roads, so Leo had to act fast. He dragged two wood benches together in the middle aisle, far from the cold outer walls. One by one, he moved the heavy clay pots to the low shelf under the planks. Next, he unrolled thick burlap blankets from the supply bin and draped them over the benches like a low tent. The cloth would trap air around the plants, but it still needed a source of heat.

Leo spotted a stack of dark clay bricks and five-gallon water jugs under the sink. During the sunny afternoon, those dark jugs had soaked up heat from the bright winter sun. Even better, a low shelf held three flat warmers used to sprout seeds. Leo plugged the seed mats into the big battery box that ran the weather gauge. He slid the warm mats and the sun-warmed water jugs right under the burlap tent.

Leo sat on a bucket beside the insulated shelter and watched the probe climb back to fifty-two degrees. The trapped warmth from the jugs and mats radiated slowly through the dark space. When the custodian arrived with a wrench to clear the ice from the gas valve at sunrise, every single tomato stem stood firm and green. Leo untied the burlap flap and smiled at the yarn tags that had made it through the night.

tier2Words.definition: fell or dropped straight down at a very fast speed
tier2Words.rootHint: Old French 'plombet' (a lead weight used to measure depth)
tier2Words.contextClue: The red line on the wall thermometer dropped fast toward thirty-five degrees after the furnace stopped.

tier2Words.definition: easily broken or damaged; fragile and requiring gentle care
tier2Words.contextClue: One hard freeze would burst the cells and ruin the fragile blossoms before dawn.

tier2Words.definition: protected with material that prevents the loss of heat
tier2Words.rootHint: Latin 'insula' (island; separated to keep energy from escaping)
tier2Words.contextClue: The burlap tent trapped warm air inside so the probe climbed back to fifty-two degrees.

tier2Words.contextClue: The trapped warmth from the jugs and mats spread slowly through the dark space.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"Halfway through the midnight storm, the main gas valve feeding the overhead furnace was abruptly snapped shut by a sheet of falling roof ice."

Based on the structure of this sentence, what actually closed the main gas valve?

options.text: The overhead furnace shut the valve off to save fuel during the storm.
Leo turned the gas valve off right before closing his field notes.
A sheet of falling roof ice struck and closed the gas valve.
The midnight storm blew open the glass panels above the furnace.

questions.provingSentenceText: Halfway through the midnight storm, the main gas valve feeding the overhead furnace was abruptly snapped shut by a sheet of falling roof ice.
questions.childTip: Look right after the verb phrase 'was abruptly snapped shut by' to find what caused the action.
questions.parentExplanation: This passive-voice sentence places the receiver ('the main gas valve') before the verb and includes the modifier 'feeding the overhead furnace.' The true actor performing the action appears after 'by': 'a sheet of falling roof ice' (Option B).

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"Leo checked the wall thermometer and felt his stomach drop as the red line plummeted toward thirty-five degrees."

What does the word "plummeted" mean as it is used in this sentence?

options.text: Dropped steeply and quickly toward a lower level
Stayed locked at the exact same number all night
Blinked on and off like a warning light
Melted the glass tube on the greenhouse wall

questions.provingSentenceText: Leo checked the wall thermometer and felt his stomach drop as the red line plummeted toward thirty-five degrees.
questions.childTip: Notice how fast frost creeps across the glass after the heater dies, making the thermometer line drop fast.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 2, the furnace stops during an ice storm and frost forms within ten minutes. The thermometer line 'plummeted toward thirty-five degrees,' meaning it dropped steeply and rapidly (Option C).

questions.prompt: Why does Leo place the five-gallon water jugs under the burlap tent in Paragraph 4?

options.text: He wants to keep the plastic jugs from freezing and cracking the sink.
He needs heavy weights to hold down the wood benches during the windstorm.
He plans to pour all five gallons of water onto the dry tomato roots before dawn.
He knows the dark jugs absorbed heat from the afternoon sun and will help warm the enclosed space.

questions.provingSentenceText: During the sunny afternoon, those dark jugs had soaked up heat from the bright winter sun.
questions.childTip: Click the sentence in Paragraph 4 that explains what the dark jugs soaked up during the sunny afternoon.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 4 explains that the dark five-gallon water jugs 'had soaked up heat from the bright winter sun' during the afternoon, so placing them inside the burlap tent helps release stored warmth around the plants (Option A).

questions.prompt: How does Paragraph 1 contribute to the overall structure of the story?

options.text: It explains why the school custodian forgot to repair the greenhouse roof before winter.
It establishes the months of careful work Leo invested in the heirloom tomatoes before the heater crisis strikes.
It proves that Brandywine tomatoes can survive subzero snowstorms without any shelter.
It describes the prizes Leo won at last year's county plant show.

questions.provingSentenceText: For four months, he had tended twelve pots of Cherokee Purple and Brandywine heirloom tomatoes for the county plant show.
questions.childTip: Think about how seeing Leo's four months of careful pollen work makes the sudden heater failure feel urgent.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 1 sets the stage and stakes of the story by showing Leo's four months of patient care and delicate cross-pollination, which makes the furnace failure in Paragraph 2 an urgent threat (Option B).

questions.prompt: PART A: Which statement best expresses a central theme of the passage?

options.text: Gas furnaces are much less reliable than battery boxes for heating large school buildings.
Heirloom vegetables should only be grown outdoors during the warmest weeks of summer.
Resourceful thinking and calm action can protect months of hard work when equipment suddenly fails.
Students should always wait for an adult to arrive before touching any greenhouse supplies.

questions.provingSentenceText: When the custodian arrived with a wrench to clear the ice from the gas valve at sunrise, every single tomato stem stood firm and green.
questions.childTip: Consider how Leo saves his four-month project by building an insulated tent with everyday science supplies.
questions.parentExplanation: Rather than panicking when the furnace fails, Leo combines benches, burlap blankets, sun-warmed water jugs, and battery-powered seed mats to save his heirloom tomatoes, showing how resourcefulness protects hard work (Option A).

questions.prompt: PART B: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "He slid the warm mats and the sun-warmed water jugs right under the burlap tent."
"He tied a tiny white yarn tag around the stem to mark the cross."
"Within ten minutes, frost began creeping like white lace across the lower glass panels."
"Sleet rattled against the sloped glass panes of the school greenhouse while Leo held a fine camel-hair brush between his fingers."

questions.provingSentenceText: He slid the warm mats and the sun-warmed water jugs right under the burlap tent.
questions.childTip: Pick the quote that shows Leo using clever supplies to heat the shelter and save his plants.
questions.parentExplanation: Option D directly illustrates Leo's resourceful action—combining sun-warmed water jugs and battery-powered seed mats inside a makeshift burlap tent—which proves the theme in Part A.
